newsitem.title: DENMARK: Minister sees economic upturn dawning in Denmark.
newsitem.headline: Minister sees economic upturn dawning in Denmark.

text.p: Unveiling a new economic survey on Monday, Danish economy minister Marianne Jelved drew a line under a period of flat growth for Denmark and then announced a new upturn.
"The latest data confirms that the period of flat economic growth is now over," Jelved said in a statement accompanying her ministry's latest economic survey.

"Production, employment and investment are all showing solid growth, international surveys indicate that Denmark experienced the second biggest rise in the European Union in industrial production in the second quarter of 1996," she said.

The economy ministry survey increased earlier expectations of gross domestic product (GDP) growth to two percent in 1996 and 3.1 percent in 1997, compared with its last survey in August in which it forecast 1.8 percent and three percent respectively.

It kept its inflation forecasts more or less unchanged at 2.1 percent this year and 2.3 percent next year, with unemployment at 8.9 percent of the workforce in 1996, falling to 8.4 percent at end-1997.
In addition the ministry said it expected Denmark's current account surplus to be 10.3 billion crowns ($1.76 billion) in 1996, rising marginally to 10.8 billion crowns next year.
The market took the new economic forecast in its stride, with the better outlook expected by most analysts and little new found in its estimates.

"It comes as no surprise to us that the government has upwardly adjusted its GDP forecasts for this year, but we fear that the estimate for 1997 is too optimistic," Nykredit Bank wrote in a comment on the new survey.
"Any general upturn in Europe is expected to be depressed by ongoing low German growth," it said.
The opposition Conservative party, which collaborated with the government in passing this year's state budget, welcomed the signs that Denmark was entering a new period of growth.

"The Danish economy is now moving into a period of growth. But major savings will still be needed if the public sector budget is to be balanced," Conservative spokeswoman Anne Birgitte Lundholdt said in a statement.
"There are positive signs but the greatest risk to the Danish economy is that wage rises get out of control in next spring's pay negotiations," Lundholdt warned.

Jelved said that Denmark now satisfied the convergence criteria for European economic and monetary union (EMU) despite the fact that it had already opted out of the project and a national referendum would have to be held on any Danish participation at a future juncture.
Jelved warned though that there were dangerous trends in Denmark's economic upturn and promised moves to curb in particular public building and construction projects.
"This is a signal that we must take seriously. To avoid any overheating of the economy, the government is taking steps to dampen public sector building programmes," she said.
She reiterated that the government's target of balancing the public sector budget in 1997 was still possible.
The survey saw the public sector deficit for this year at 14.9 billion crowns, falling to a manageable 3.5 billion crowns next year.

"A balanced 1997 public sector budget is within our grasp and this will be one of the government's main targets to be realised in the upcoming negotiations with opposition parties on the 1997 state budget," Jelved stressed.
Economist Soeren Nielsen at the fourth biggest bank Jyske Bank said he found the economy ministry's public sector forecast realistic.
"The public sector deficit next year depends in the main on how the upcoming negotiations on next year's state budget go," Nielsen told Reuters.

Denmark's 1997 state budget is to be passed by Christmas following negotiations between the Social Democrat-led centre-left minority government and opposition parties due to start this month. ($1=5.865 Danish Crown)
